title: TCP connection states
summary: The state machine behind every socket, and what TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT piles are telling you.

steps.title: The state machine
body: opening                               closing (the side that closes first is "active")
CLOSED --listen--> LISTEN             ESTABLISHED --close--> FIN_WAIT_1 --rcv ACK--> FIN_WAIT_2
LISTEN --rcv SYN--> SYN_RECEIVED      FIN_WAIT_2 --rcv FIN--> TIME_WAIT --2*MSL--> CLOSED
SYN_SENT --rcv SYN-ACK--> ESTABLISHED ESTABLISHED --rcv FIN--> CLOSE_WAIT --close--> LAST_ACK
SYN_RECEIVED --rcv ACK--> ESTABLISHED LAST_ACK --rcv ACK--> CLOSED
Closing takes four segments, because each direction is shut separately: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK.

steps.prompt: Order a normal close where the client closes first.
lines: Server app closes and sends FIN (server: LAST_ACK)
Client waits 2 x MSL, then CLOSED
steps.explain: The active closer ends up in TIME_WAIT.

steps.title: TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT
body: **TIME_WAIT** lasts 2 × the maximum segment lifetime (60 s on Linux). It makes sure the last ACK can be resent and that stray old segments die before the same port pair is reused.

Thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets on a busy client are normal, but they can exhaust ephemeral ports when one host opens many short connections to the same server: reuse connections (keep-alive, pooling, one `HttpClient`).
**CLOSE_WAIT** means the peer closed, and **your application hasn't called close yet**. A growing pile of CLOSE_WAIT is almost always a bug: a leaked socket.
ss -tanp state close-wait          # -p shows the owning process

steps.prompt: A .NET service shows 4,000 sockets in `CLOSE_WAIT` to the database, growing all day. What's going on?
options: The app isn't disposing connections after the database closes them: a resource leak in the code
steps.explain: CLOSE_WAIT is waiting on *your* close(). Look for missing `using`/`Dispose`.

steps.prompt: Which side passes through which state?
Complete the commands: count TIME_WAIT sockets, then list the CLOSE_WAIT sockets with the process that owns each one.
steps.explain: `-p` shows which process owns each socket: the one leaking connections.

steps.title: The TCP state machine
prompt: Write a class `TcpConnection` with `string State` (starts `"CLOSED"`) and `string Handle(string evt)` that applies a transition and returns the new state.
Events: `listen`, `connect`, `rcv SYN`, `rcv SYN-ACK`, `rcv ACK`, `close`, `rcv FIN`, `timeout`. Implement exactly the transitions in the diagram (`timeout` is the 2*MSL timer that ends TIME_WAIT),
plus `FIN_WAIT_1 --rcv FIN--> CLOSING` and `CLOSING --rcv ACK--> TIME_WAIT` (simultaneous close). Anything else throws `InvalidOperationException`.
starter: public string State { get; private set; } = "CLOSED";
solution: public string State { get; private set; } = "CLOSED";
private static readonly Dictionary<(string, string), string> Transitions = new()
throw new InvalidOperationException($"{evt} not valid in {State}");
template: dojoC.Handle("connect"); dojoC.Handle("rcv SYN-ACK"); dojoC.Handle("close"); dojoC.Handle("rcv ACK");
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("can't close a closed socket", () => new TcpConnection().Handle("close"));
hints: A dictionary keyed by `(state, event)` tuples keeps it readable.
Throw when the pair isn't in the table.

steps.title: Summarise ss output
prompt: Write `Dictionary<string, int> Count(List<string> ssLines)` counting sockets per state from `ss -tan` output (first word of each line).
Skip the header line (it starts with `State`) and blank lines.
template: "State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port",
